person.name: Franz_Kafka
person.summary: Franz Kafka (1883–1924) was a German-language Jewish writer from Prague whose unsettling, precise prose reshaped 20th‑century literature. Trained as a lawyer and employed in insurance, he wrote fiction in his spare hours, portraying isolated protagonists trapped in opaque bureaucratic systems. Only a handful of works, including "The Metamorphosis" and the story collections "Contemplation" and "A Country Doctor", appeared during his lifetime, but they influenced generations of writers, philosophers, and artists. His early death from tuberculosis left his novels unfinished and his reputation to grow posthumously from near-obscurity to global prominence.

events.title: Birth in Prague
events.description: Franz Kafka is born into a German-speaking Jewish middle‑class family in Prague, then part of the Austro‑Hungarian Empire. His father, Hermann Kafka, is a self‑made haberdasher, while his mother, Julie, comes from a more educated mercantile family and works long hours in the family business. The household is marked by the parents’ frequent absence and the presence of governesses and servants, circumstances that later inform Kafka’s depictions of emotional distance and authority.

images.caption: Plaque marking Franz Kafka’s birthplace in Prague
images.creator: Godot13

events.title: Schooling and early anxieties
events.description: From 1889 Kafka attends a German boys’ elementary school and then the rigorous Altstädter Deutsches Gymnasium in Prague’s Old Town. He excels academically but is plagued by intense fear of failure and by his father’s harsh expectations, experiences that later echo in his portraits of oppressive authority. Around 1899 he briefly embraces socialism, even wearing a red carnation in his buttonhole, and in 1901 passes his [[Matura|Matura]] exams and travels outside Bohemia for the first time with his uncle Siegfried Löwy. These years establish both his intellectual ambitions and his enduring sense of inner insecurity.

Matura.explanation: Final secondary-school examinations in parts of Central and Eastern Europe (including the former Austro-Hungarian lands), required for university entrance.

events.title: Studies law at Prague university
events.description: In 1901 Kafka matriculates at the German [[Charles‑Ferdinand University|Charles‑Ferdinand University]] in [[Prague|Prague]], initially enrolling in chemistry before switching to law, a choice that satisfies his father and offers practical career prospects. He joins the [[Lese- und Redehalle der deutschen Studenten|Lese- und Redehalle der deutschen Studenten]], where he attends literary events and forges close friendships with Max Brod, Felix Weltsch, Oskar Baum, and other members of the later "Prague Circle." Alongside his law courses he listens to lectures on philosophy, German literature, and art history, while reading writers such as Flaubert, Dostoevsky, and Gogol. On 18 June 1906 he receives his Doctor of Law degree and proceeds to an obligatory year as a law clerk in the civil and criminal courts of Prague.

Charles‑Ferdinand University.explanation: The German Charles‑Ferdinand University was the German-language branch of Prague’s historic Charles University, serving the city’s German-speaking population in the Austro‑Hungarian period.

Prague.explanation: At the time of Kafka’s studies, Prague was the capital of the Kingdom of Bohemia within the Austro‑Hungarian Empire and had distinct German- and Czech-speaking cultural spheres.

Lese- und Redehalle der deutschen Studen.explanation: The Lese- und Redehalle der deutschen Studenten was a German-speaking student reading and debating society in Prague that functioned as a cultural and literary club for university students.

events.title: First insurance job in Prague
events.description: On 1 November 1907 Kafka begins full‑time work at the Italian insurance firm [[Assicurazioni Generali|Assicurazioni Generali]] in Prague. The long office hours, often from early morning until evening, leave little time for writing and quickly exhaust him. His letters from this period already contrast the demands of salaried work with his longing to devote himself entirely to literature. Feeling trapped, he resigns on 15 July 1908, resolving to find a position more compatible with his literary ambitions.

Assicurazioni Generali.explanation: Assicurazioni Generali is a large Italian insurance company, founded in 1831 in Trieste, that expanded across Central and Eastern Europe in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

events.title: Career at Workers’ Accident Insurance Institute
events.description: Within weeks of leaving Assicurazioni Generali, Kafka joins the [[Workers’ Accident Insurance Institute for the Kingdom of Bohemia|Workers’ Accident Insurance Institute for the Kingdom of Bohemia]], a semi‑state body responsible for industrial accident insurance. Over the next fourteen years he investigates factory accidents, drafts technical reports and safety regulations, and is repeatedly promoted, eventually becoming Obersekretär. World War I brings him into contact with wounded veterans and eastern Jewish refugees, and the Institute has him work on rehabilitation schemes rather than at the front. Though he calls the post his "bread job" and resents its encroachment on his writing time, the bureaucratic routines and power structures he encounters here profoundly shape the atmospheres of "The Trial" and "The Castle."

images.caption: Former Workers’ Accident Insurance Institute building, Prague
images.creator: alphabet55

Workers’ Accident Insurance Institute fo.explanation: A semi-public insurance institution based in Prague that administered compulsory accident insurance for industrial workers in the Kingdom of Bohemia, where Kafka worked as a legal and technical expert from 1908 to 1922.

events.title: First literary publications
events.description: In 1908 Kafka’s first prose pieces appear in print when the Munich journal Hyperion publishes a group of short texts later collected under the title "Contemplation." Encouraged by Max Brod, he continues revising and submitting stories, gradually gaining confidence in his vocation as a writer even while keeping his literary ambitions largely hidden from his family. These early sketches, with their precise yet disquieting observations of everyday life, anticipate the tone of his mature work. They also establish him, within a small avant‑garde readership, as part of the emerging German‑language literature of Prague.

events.title: Immerses in Yiddish theatre
events.description: In the autumn of 1911 Kafka encounters a [[Yiddish theatre|Yiddish theatre]] troupe performing in Prague and is captivated by their language and intensity. He befriends the actor Jizchak Löwy, helps organize a recitation evening, and for several months throws himself into Yiddish plays and stories. This immersion renews his connection to Jewish tradition and prompts him to reflect on the contrast between assimilated Western Jews and the more overtly religious culture he sees on stage. The experience feeds into his evolving sense of identity and leaves traces in later texts that evoke itinerant performers and marginal communities.

Yiddish theatre.explanation: Professional or semi-professional theatrical performances in the Yiddish language, which flourished among Eastern European Jewish communities and often combined melodrama, music, and religious or folk themes.

events.title: Meets Felice Bauer and breakthrough night
events.description: On 13 August 1912 Kafka meets Felice Bauer, a Berlin office professional visiting the home of Max Brod’s family in Prague; within days he begins an intense, mostly epistolary courtship that will lead to two engagements and repeated ruptures. During this emotionally charged period he experiences a creative breakthrough: in a single night, 22–23 September 1912, he writes the story "The Judgment," which he dedicates to Felice. In the following years he drafts major sections of the novel later titled "Amerika" and, in 1912–1913, the novella "The Metamorphosis." The tangled hopes and fears surrounding marriage and autonomy in his relationship with Felice deeply inform the themes of these works.

events.title: Publishes "The Metamorphosis"
events.description: In 1915 the expressionist journal [[Die Weißen Blätter|Die Weißen Blätter]] publishes Kafka’s novella "The Metamorphosis," in which the traveling salesman Gregor Samsa wakes up transformed into a monstrous vermin. Written while Kafka continues his demanding insurance work and struggles with his engagement to Felice Bauer, the story distills his preoccupations with family guilt, bodily estrangement, and mute suffering. Contemporary reception is modest, but within a small circle of readers the text is recognized as strikingly original. It will later become one of the most discussed and emblematic narratives of 20th‑century literature.

images.caption: First edition of Kafka’s novella “Die Verwandlung”
images.creator: © Foto H.-P.Haack

Die Weißen Blätter.explanation: A German expressionist literary journal, published in Leipzig, that served as an important early outlet for avant‑garde writing in the 1910s.

events.title: Tuberculosis diagnosis and Zürau retreat
events.description: In August 1917 Kafka suffers a severe lung hemorrhage and is diagnosed with tuberculosis, forcing him to take extended leave from the insurance institute. He moves to the rural village of Zürau (Siřem), where his sister Ottla and her husband manage a farm, and spends several months living quietly in the countryside. Free for the first time from both office work and urban pressures, he fills notebooks with reflections and aphorisms later known as the Zürau Aphorisms. Although physically ill, he later recalls this period as one of the most peaceful and creatively focused of his life.

events.title: Relationship with Milena Jesenská
events.description: Around 1920 Kafka enters into an intense relationship with the Czech journalist and translator Milena Jesenská, who is married and lives mostly in Vienna. After she translates his story "The Stoker" into Czech, their correspondence quickly deepens into a passionate and tormented exchange about love, illness, and self‑doubt. Kafka visits her in person only a few times, but the emotional strain of the affair, combined with his worsening health, contributes to the eventual break in late 1920. The letters he writes to Milena, later published posthumously, offer some of the most revealing insights into his inner life and his view of his own writing.

images.caption: Villa Ottoburg in Meran-Untermais where Kafka stayed
images.creator: Zintosch7

events.title: Retires from insurance work
events.description: On 1 July 1922 the Workers’ Accident Insurance Institute finally grants Kafka a pension on medical grounds, releasing him from regular employment. By this point his tuberculosis and chronic exhaustion make sustained office work impossible, yet he continues to write when his health allows, working on the novel "The Castle" and revising stories. Financially dependent on his family and friends, he shuttles between Prague and various sanatoriums in the Bohemian countryside. The separation from salaried work intensifies both his sense of marginality and his determination to shape his remaining prose.

events.title: Life with Dora Diamant in Berlin
events.description: During a seaside holiday at [[Graal-Müritz|Graal‑Müritz]] in July 1923, Kafka meets Dora Diamant, a young woman from an orthodox Jewish background working with children at a holiday camp. Seeking distance from his family and a space devoted to writing, he moves with her to Berlin in September, and the couple share modest flats while he studies Hebrew and tentatively plans a future in Palestine. Despite poverty and his deteriorating health, this partnership brings him emotional support and a renewed engagement with Jewish texts and traditions. In these months he completes several stories later collected under the title "A Hunger Artist."

Graal-Müritz.explanation: Graal-Müritz is a Baltic Sea resort town in northern Germany that developed in the late 19th and early 20th centuries as a seaside health and holiday destination, popular with urban middle‑class visitors.

events.title: Death in Kierling sanatorium
events.description: Kafka’s throat tuberculosis worsens in early 1924, making eating agonizing and forcing his transfer from Berlin back to Prague and then to a sanatorium in Kierling near Vienna. There Dora Diamant and his sister Ottla help care for him as he corrects the proofs of "A Hunger Artist" even on his sickbed. Unable to take sufficient nourishment and with no effective medical treatment available, he dies on 3 June 1924 at the age of forty. His body is returned to Prague and buried in the New Jewish Cemetery, leaving behind mostly unpublished manuscripts that his friend Max Brod will later edit and bring to world attention.
